episode_title: S2 Ep23: The Retail Shift: Exploring the changing landscape of Australian retail with Dean Salakas

real_qa.q: How did Dean Salakas become Australia's first click and collect retailer in 1999?
real_qa.r: While in high school in 1999, Dean Salakas launched The Party People business online, which made it Australia's first retailer to offer click and collect functionality. He later discovered Google AdWords coming to Australia in 2003 during a university project and became Google AdWords' first advertiser, paying one cent per click.
real_qa.requete: Dean Salakas Australia first click and collect 1999

real_qa.q: What is the key difference between how The Party People positioned itself versus competitors?
real_qa.r: Dean positioned The Party People not as a business selling party products, but as a business helping people have the parties they dream about. He explains: 'Everyone thought they were in the business of selling party products. I looked at it that I was in the business of helping people have parties.' This distinction influenced every strategic decision, including offering services that don't make money but help customers have parties.
real_qa.requete: Party People business model problem solving strategy

real_qa.q: How many members does the Australian retail community WhatsApp group have that Dean Salakas built?
real_qa.r: Dean started a WhatsApp chat with Jethro Marks at a conference to organize drinks. The chat group grew to 100 people by the end of the first day, 300 by the end of the conference, and now has 4,000+ members 18 months later, becoming his primary focus.
real_qa.requete: Dean Salakas retail community WhatsApp 4000 members

real_qa.q: What role do robots play in inventory management at major Australian retailers like Kmart and Bunnings?
real_qa.r: Robots that look like RoboVacs with a pole on top are now counting inventory in stores at Kmart and Bunnings. These robots look at inventory levels on every shelf and perform inventory counts every night, effectively replacing stock takers in these stores.
real_qa.requete: robots inventory Kmart Bunnings Australia retail automation

real_qa.q: How did The Party People differentiate its in-store experience from competitors?
real_qa.r: Customers walking into The Party People were immediately hit with a 'wow factor.' The store had balloons everywhere, decorations, and displays packed to the roof at eight meters high, making the space visually appealing. Dean explains: 'People judge you on your first five seconds like a person. The store's the same. They judge you as soon as they walk in.' This immediate visual impact created a strong first impression.
real_qa.requete: Party People store experience design retail retail wow factor

real_qa.q: What are the main challenges small retailers face competing against Amazon, Shein, and Temu in Australia?
real_qa.r: Dean says buying customers through digital advertising is difficult as a primary strategy, though it should be part of the mix. The real answer is having an amazing product that solves a customer problem better than anyone else, combined with making noise about what you do through media and PR. He emphasizes: 'You've got to have a great product that solves a problem. And you've got to make sure everyone knows about it. And you can't have one without the other.'
real_qa.requete: small retailers compete Amazon Shein Temu Australia strategy

guest.bio_context: Dean Salakas grew up working in The Party People, a family business started by his mother as a party supplies retailer. In 1999 while in high school, he launched the business online and became Australia's first retailer to offer click and collect. In 2003, he became Google AdWords' first advertiser in Australia, paying one cent per click. He worked at Woolworths as a business analyst while growing The Party People part-time, acquiring the business with his brother in 2007. After triple-digit growth and multiple acquisitions, he exited The Party People in December 2024 and now focuses on building a retail community that has grown to 4,000+ members in 18 months.

real_quote: Everyone thought they were in the business of selling party products. I looked at it that I was in the business of helping people have parties.

2003: year Google AdWords launched in Australia, with Dean Salakas as first advertiser paying one cent per click
2007: year Dean Salakas and his brother acquired The Party People from their mother
December 2024: month and year of final exit when buyer acquired remaining stake of The Party People
4,000+ members: size of Australian retail WhatsApp community 18 months after Dean started it
8 meters: height of The Party People store roof filled with product and displays
